sentence: And—but inflation expectations did not move strongly down here in the United States.
Again, that’s not a forecast, I’ve made a hypothesis, which would imply slower improvement in unemployment.
So for many, many years, we’ve been far from maximum employment and stable prices, and so the need for accommodative policy has been—has been clear.
You know, it’s interest rates, it’s risk spreads, it’s currency, it’s the stock market, it’s credit availability, it’s many, many factors.

By getting unemployment down, we hope to bring back to work some of the people who’ve been out of work as long as they have and, in that respect, try to avoid the longer-term consequences of people being out of work for months at a time.
Inflation has moved up in recent months, mainly reflecting higher prices for some commodities and imported goods.

So, I think you raise a very important point because, although there is a great deal of market focus on the timing of liftoff, what to matter in thinking about the stance of policy is what the entire path of interest rates will look like.

For example, we have used some of our work to look at interest rate risk and interest rate sensitivity and, you know, found generally that banks can also sustain a significant increase in long-term interest rates as well for a number of reasons, one of them being that higher interest rates increase their franchise value because it increases their net interest margin over time.
We have a 2 percent symmetric inflation objective, and, for a number of years now, inflation has been running under 2 percent.
And downward revisions to the longer-run normal unemployment rate in a way suggests that participants are seeing more slack in the economy now than they previously did.
So, with this coronavirus arriving, we judged that the—the net effects of this will be to—to have inflation move down even a little bit more.
We understand that inflation dynamics evolve constantly over time, but they don’t change rapidly.
Monetary policy has a role, and it really is in, you know—our original role was providing liquidity to financial systems when they’re under stress, and that’s—that’s really part of what we did today.
And so you’re seeing prices are moving back up off their lows there.

So, if we maintain a highly accommodative monetary policy for a very long time from here and the economy performs as we expect—namely, it’s strong and the risks that are out there don’t materialize—my concern will be that we will have much more tightening in labor markets than you see in these projections.
It also affects stock prices.
So there’s been a number of emerging markets—as you know, we’re suffering under the weight of declines in oil prices that are affecting their economic activity.

And, at a high level, yes, I would say, and I’ve said before, that it’s really fiscal policy that is more powerful and that has much more to do with—fiscal policy can do those things that will increase the longer-run growth rate of the United States by improving productivity and labor force September 18, 2019 participation and the skills and aptitudes of workers.
These headwinds—which include developments abroad, subdued household formation, and meager productivity growth—could persist for some time.
Monetary policy, maximum employment, stable prices—it’s less obvious to me.
So you’re right, you’re seeing—I, I can’t remember the number, but it might be in the 3s—3, 3½ percent growth for next year.
Our role, though, is also to, you know, to make sure that—that maximum employment happens in a context of price stability and financial stability, which is why we’re gradually raising rates.

Smoothing through these variations, average monthly job growth appears to have stepped down from last year’s strong pace, but job gains remain well above the pace necessary to provide jobs for new labor force entrants.
That’s not going to happen without, without restoring price stability.
